questions.question: A distributed cache uses modulo hashing (hash(key) % N) with 4 nodes. If a 5th node is added, approximately what percentage of keys need to be remapped?

options.text: 20% (only keys that would map to the new node)
25% (one quarter of keys redistributed)
80% (most keys hash to different nodes when N changes)
100% (all keys must be recalculated)

questions.explanation: With modulo hashing, adding a node changes N in the formula, causing most keys to hash to different nodes. Approximately (N)/(N+1) = 4/5 = 80% of keys are remapped. This is why modulo hashing scales poorly. Memcached originally used modulo hashing, and adding servers caused massive cache miss storms. This problem motivated the invention of consistent hashing by Karger et al. at MIT in 1997, originally for web caching (Akamai).

questions.question: In consistent hashing, what is the primary purpose of virtual nodes (vnodes)?

options.text: To increase the total storage capacity of the cluster
To achieve more uniform data distribution across physical nodes
To provide backup copies of data for fault tolerance
To reduce network latency by localizing related keys

questions.explanation: Virtual nodes give each physical node multiple positions on the hash ring, smoothing out distribution imbalances. Without vnodes, nodes with unlucky hash positions might receive disproportionate load. A node at position 0.1 on a 0-1 ring would get 10% of keys if the next node is at 0.2, but 50% if the next node is at 0.6. Cassandra uses 256 vnodes per node by default. DynamoDB uses a similar concept. The tradeoff: more vnodes means better distribution but more metadata to track.

questions.question: A consistent hashing ring has nodes A, B, C, D positioned clockwise. Node B fails. Which statement is true about key redistribution?

options.text: All keys are redistributed evenly across A, C, and D
Only keys that were on B move to the next node clockwise (C)
Keys are redistributed based on load balancing algorithms
B's keys are split between its neighbors A and C

questions.explanation: In consistent hashing, only keys belonging to the failed node move. They go to the next node clockwise on the ring (C in this case). Other nodes' keys are unaffected, minimizing redistribution. This is the key advantage over modulo hashing. When a Cassandra node fails, only 1/N of the data needs to move (where N is the number of nodes), not the 80%+ that modulo hashing would require. This property enables graceful scaling and failure handling.

questions.question: Which problems does consistent hashing solve? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Minimizing key redistribution when nodes are added or removed
Guaranteeing perfectly equal data distribution across all nodes
Enabling horizontal scaling of distributed caches and databases
Eliminating the need for a central coordinator to locate data

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing minimizes remapping (only K/N keys move when adding a node, where K is total keys and N is nodes), enables scaling (add/remove nodes with minimal disruption), and allows decentralized key location (any client can compute which node owns a key). It does NOT guarantee perfect distribution. That is why virtual nodes are used to improve uniformity. Even with vnodes, hot keys can still cause imbalance. Consistent hashing solves the scaling problem, not the hot-spot problem.

questions.question: A distributed database uses consistent hashing with a replication factor of 3. How are replicas typically placed?

options.text: On three randomly selected nodes for load distribution
On the three nodes clockwise from the key's hash position on the ring
On the primary node plus two designated backup nodes
On nodes in three different data centers regardless of ring position

questions.explanation: Replicas are placed on consecutive nodes clockwise from the key's position on the ring. This ensures replicas are deterministically located (any node can calculate replica locations) and spread across different nodes for fault tolerance. Cassandra, DynamoDB, and Riak all use this approach. The deterministic placement is crucial. Without it, you would need a central coordinator to track replica locations, reintroducing a single point of failure.

questions.question: What happens in consistent hashing when a new node joins the ring?

options.text: All existing data is rebalanced across all nodes for even distribution
The new node takes over a portion of keys from its clockwise neighbor only
No data movement occurs until an administrator triggers rebalancing
The ring must be rebuilt from scratch with new hash assignments

questions.explanation: The new node takes responsibility for keys between itself and its predecessor on the ring. Only those keys move from the successor node. Other nodes are unaffected, enabling smooth scaling. When you add a node to a Cassandra cluster, it streams data only from its new neighbors, not from the entire cluster. This is why consistent hashing enables online scaling. You can add capacity without taking the system offline or causing massive data movement.

questions.question: A system uses consistent hashing with 100 virtual nodes per physical node. If there are 10 physical nodes, how many points are on the hash ring?

options.text: 10 (one per physical node)
100 (virtual nodes are shared)
1,000 (100 vnodes times 10 physical nodes)
110 (physical nodes plus virtual nodes)

questions.explanation: Each physical node has 100 virtual nodes, so 10 times 100 = 1,000 points on the ring. More points generally means better distribution uniformity because the law of large numbers smooths out random placement. Cassandra defaults to 256 vnodes per node. With a 100-node cluster, that is 25,600 points on the ring, providing very even distribution. The tradeoff is metadata size and lookup time, though modern implementations handle this efficiently.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of using too many virtual nodes per physical node?

options.text: Worse data distribution due to hash collisions
Increased memory overhead for ring metadata and longer ring traversal
Slower hash computation for each key lookup
Reduced fault tolerance due to replica co-location

questions.explanation: Each virtual node requires storage in the ring metadata. With many vnodes across many physical nodes, the ring structure consumes significant memory and takes longer to traverse for lookups. Cassandra reduced its default from 256 to 16 vnodes in version 4.0 partly for this reason. The ring metadata must be replicated to all nodes for decentralized lookups. With 1000 nodes and 256 vnodes each, that is 256,000 entries every node must store and keep synchronized.

questions.question: A common claim is that consistent hashing guarantees even data distribution. Under what circumstances is this claim FALSE?

options.text: When using fewer than 100 virtual nodes per physical node
When key distribution is non-uniform (hot keys or skewed access patterns)
When nodes have different storage capacities
All of the above can cause uneven distribution

questions.explanation: Basic consistent hashing can result in uneven distribution due to random node placement (few vnodes), hot keys (some keys accessed far more than others), and heterogeneous hardware (a node with 2x storage should get 2x keys). Virtual nodes improve uniformity but do not guarantee it. Hot keys remain hot regardless of placement. Weighted consistent hashing addresses heterogeneous nodes by giving larger nodes more vnodes. But fundamentally, consistent hashing solves the scaling problem, not the hot-spot problem.

questions.question: A CDN uses consistent hashing to route requests to edge servers. A server fails and is removed. What is the impact on cache hit rate?

options.text: Cache hit rate drops to zero temporarily across all content
Only requests that would have gone to the failed server experience cache misses
All cached content must be re-fetched from origin servers
Cache hit rate is unaffected due to automatic failover

questions.explanation: Only keys that were assigned to the failed server are affected. They will miss cache on the new server until re-cached. Other servers retain their cached content, minimizing overall impact. This is why Akamai, Cloudflare, and other CDNs use consistent hashing. If a server fails, only 1/N of requests see cache misses, not 100%. The origin servers see a small spike in traffic, not a thundering herd. This graceful degradation is essential for CDN reliability.

questions.question: Which systems commonly use consistent hashing? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB for partition key distribution
Apache Cassandra for data partitioning
PostgreSQL for table partitioning
Memcached with ketama algorithm

questions.explanation: DynamoDB, Cassandra, and Memcached (ketama algorithm) use consistent hashing for data distribution. PostgreSQL uses range or list partitioning, not consistent hashing. It is designed for single-node or primary-replica setups, not the peer-to-peer distribution that consistent hashing enables. The distinction: consistent hashing is for distributing data across a cluster of peers; traditional partitioning is for organizing data within a single logical database.

questions.question: In consistent hashing, what determines which node is responsible for a given key?

options.text: The node with the smallest hash value in the cluster
The first node encountered when traversing clockwise from the key's hash position
A central coordinator that maintains a key-to-node mapping table
The node that currently has the most available storage capacity

questions.explanation: Keys are assigned to the first node found when traversing clockwise from the key's hash position on the ring. This deterministic assignment allows any client to locate data without central coordination. Hash the key, find its position on the ring, walk clockwise to the first node. This is O(log N) with a sorted list of node positions or O(1) with a jump consistent hash variant. The decentralization is key: no single point of failure for routing decisions.
